subtitle: The most musical and dynamic form of distortion. Overdrive pedals add warmth, sustain, and natural tube-like compression to your guitar tone.

introduction.title: What is Overdrive?
introduction.text: Overdrive is a form of audio signal distortion that occurs naturally when an amplifier is driven beyond its clean headroom, and overdrive pedals exist mainly to recreate that same soft, amp-like clipping at any volume rather than only once a tube amp is cranked loud enough to break up on its own. Because the clipping is gradual rather than an abrupt ceiling, an overdrive pedal keeps responding to how hard you pick and how far you turn the guitar's volume knob, which is exactly the touch-sensitivity a harder-clipping distortion circuit gives up in exchange for consistency.

columns.title: Characteristics
columns.text: An overdrive pedal clips the peaks of the waveform softly, rounding them off rather than flattening them the way a distortion pedal does, and that gentler clipping preserves much more of the original note's fundamental pitch and harmonic makeup. Because the onset of clipping is gradual instead of a fixed ceiling, the effect stays genuinely touch-sensitive: pick softly and the signal stays closer to clean, dig in and the same pedal saturates further, all without touching a single knob.

columns.title: Musical Applications
columns.text: That responsiveness to touch is why overdrive, rather than distortion, is the default choice for blues and classic rock rhythm playing, styles built around dynamic variation from note to note rather than a uniformly saturated wall of gain. The same gentle clipping is what makes overdrive the standard way to push an already slightly-driven tube amp further into its own natural breakup, and why stacking a low-gain overdrive in front of a second drive pedal, rather than just turning one pedal's gain up, is a common way to shape tone in stages instead of all at once.

cards.title: Tube-Style Circuits
cards.description: Rather than using actual vacuum tubes, most overdrive pedals run an op-amp circuit into a pair of diodes, which clip the signal in a way that mimics a tube's soft, gradual saturation far more cheaply and reliably than fitting a real tube into a battery-powered stompbox would. Using two slightly mismatched diodes, an asymmetrical arrangement, produces uneven clipping on the positive and negative halves of the waveform, generating the same even-order harmonics a real tube amp produces and giving the pedal its warmer, more "tube-like" character compared to symmetrical clipping.

fields.label: Others
fields.value: Some include bass, presence, or mid controls

cards.title: Transparent Overdrive
cards.description: A transparent overdrive is designed to add gain and sustain while coloring the underlying tone as little as possible, so a bright guitar stays bright and a dark-sounding amp stays dark rather than the pedal imposing its own EQ signature on top. That neutrality is exactly what makes these pedals effective as a way to push an already-good clean or edge-of-breakup amp tone harder, since the goal is more of what the amp is already doing rather than a new flavor layered over it.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Boss OD-1, Ibanez TS808, Xotic EP Booster

cards.title: Colored Overdrive
cards.description: A colored overdrive is built around a specific voicing rather than staying out of the way of your existing tone, actively shaping the frequency response and clipping character to sound a particular way regardless of what amp it's plugged into. That built-in personality is the point rather than a flaw: it's what lets one of these pedals put a recognizable, consistent character on a rig, rather than the more chameleon-like behavior of a transparent overdrive.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Boss Blues Breaker, ProCo RAT, DOD 250

cards.title: Tube Screamer Style
cards.description: The Tube Screamer circuit rolls off bass frequencies before the clipping stage and boosts the midrange afterward, which is why it tightens up a loose low end and pushes the guitar's midrange forward rather than adding raw thickness. That EQ curve is exactly what a note needs to cut through a dense band mix without turning muddy, which is why this specific topology, rather than overdrive in general, became the default boost pedal for so many working guitarists.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Ibanez TS9, Boss SD-1, Maxon OD808

cards.title: Vintage-Style
cards.description: A vintage-style overdrive is built around the specific circuit of an amp or pedal from the '70s or '80s rather than a modern general-purpose drive design, chasing the particular clipping curve and frequency response of one historical unit instead of aiming for a broadly useful tone. That focus makes them less flexible than a transparent or Tube Screamer-style pedal, but far more convincing at recreating one specific era or amplifier's breakup character than a general-purpose circuit designed to work well with anything.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Marshall Blues Breaker, Boss OD-3, Fulltone OCD

cards.title: Ibanez Tube Screamer (TS808/TS9)
cards.description: The most influential overdrive pedal ever made. Known for its smooth midrange focus and ability to make any amp sound better. Used by Stevie Ray Vaughan, Gary Moore, and countless blues and rock legends.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Mid-range focused, smooth clipping, tight low end, perfect for blues and lead tones

cards.title: Boss Blues Breaker (BB-2)
cards.description: Based on the Marshall Blues Breaker amplifier, this pedal delivers vintage British overdrive tones. More open and less compressed than Tube Screamers.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Open, transparent overdrive with British character and natural dynamics

items: John Mayer - Clean boost and overdrive

cards.title: ProCo RAT 2
cards.description: Technically a distortion pedal, but often used as a high-gain overdrive. Known for its aggressive midrange and ability to cut through dense mixes.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Aggressive, midrange-heavy overdrive with great note definition and sustain

cards.title: Technique Tips
cards.description: Because overdrive clips gradually rather than at a fixed ceiling, most of its dynamic range lives in your hands rather than on the pedal's dial. Rolling the guitar's volume back cleans up the tone almost like bypassing the pedal, and picking harder pushes further into saturation, which is why players who rely on overdrive tend to touch the guitar's own controls constantly instead of setting the pedal once and leaving it.
items: Use guitar volume knob for dynamics
Set drive level for touch sensitivity
Adjust amp EQ with overdrive engaged
Use moderate gain for best note clarity

cards.title: Stacking & Combinations
cards.description: Running a low-gain overdrive into a second, higher-gain drive pedal shapes the tone in stages rather than all at once: the first pedal's soft clipping smooths and compresses the signal slightly before it ever reaches the second pedal's own clipping stage, which produces a thicker, more layered saturation than simply turning one pedal's gain all the way up. This is also why a low-gain overdrive works as a clean boost in front of an already-driven amp: set with its own gain low, it acts mostly as a volume and midrange push into the amp's front end rather than adding audible clipping of its own.
items: Stack two overdrives for more gain
Use lower gain OD to push higher gain OD
Combine with fuzz for unique textures
Use as clean boost (drive at minimum)
Push tube amps into natural saturation

sections.title: Overdrive Settings Guide
sections.warningText: Start with all controls at noon, then adjust to taste. Remember that overdrive pedals interact heavily with your amp's preamp, so adjust both together for optimal results.
